subtitle: Master the natural, organic sound of acoustic guitars

introduction.title: Acoustic Guitars: Pure, Natural Sound
introduction.text: An acoustic guitar makes its entire sound from a vibrating string driving a wooden soundboard, with no pickup, amp, or power supply required. That simplicity is precisely why it has stayed central to songwriting and performance for over a century: you can pick one up anywhere, in any room, and it projects on its own. The trade-off is that everything about how it's built — body size, top wood, bracing — has a direct, audible effect on tone, since there's no electronics downstream to compensate for a weak-sounding instrument.

columns.title: What Makes Acoustics Special
columns.text: An acoustic's sound comes entirely from wood resonating in response to the string, which is why two guitars with identical strings and setup can still sound completely different depending on their top and body. That same self-contained design is what makes the instrument so portable and immediate — no power outlet, no amp, no signal chain between you and the sound, just an instrument that projects on its own wherever you happen to be playing it.

cards.title: Steel-String Acoustics
cards.description: Steel strings put far more tension and high-frequency energy into the top than nylon does, which is what gives steel-string acoustics their bright, cutting edge and lets them hold their own in a full band mix without amplification. That same tension is why the tone holds up whether you're picking gently or strumming hard, making the steel-string the default choice across most popular genres rather than a specialist instrument for one style.
items: Bright, crisp tone: Steel strings provide clarity and punch
Strong projection: Cuts through mix in band settings
Versatile dynamics: From gentle fingerpicking to aggressive strumming
Genre flexibility: Folk, country, rock, pop, blues

cards.title: Playing Styles
cards.description: The same steel-string acoustic can sound like four different instruments depending on how you approach the strings, because strumming, fingerpicking, flatpicking, and percussive tapping each excite the top in a different way. Learning more than one of these techniques is what lets a single guitar cover rhythm accompaniment, intricate solo arrangements, and driving lead lines without ever switching instruments.
items: Strumming: Rhythm guitar for songs and accompaniment
Fingerpicking: Intricate melodies and complex arrangements
Flatpicking: Leads and fast bluegrass-style picking
Percussive: Body tapping and rhythm techniques

cards.title: Body Shapes
cards.description: Body shape changes tone mainly by changing how much air the guitar moves and where its resonant peak sits: a large dreadnought or jumbo has more internal air volume and pushes out strong bass and volume, while a smaller parlor or concert body resonates faster and emphasizes midrange over low end. That's why the same set of strings and the same player can sound noticeably different moving between body shapes — the wood hasn't changed, but the cavity that's amplifying it has.
items: Dreadnought: Largest body, powerful bass response, versatile
Concert/Auditorium: Balanced tone, comfortable for smaller players
Grand Auditorium: Great for fingerpicking, balanced across frequencies
Parlor: Vintage feel, focused midrange, great for recording
Jumbo: Maximum volume and projection, bold sound

cards.title: Wood Types
cards.description: The top wood does most of the tonal work on an acoustic guitar because it's the piece actually driven by string vibration, which is why builders talk about spruce versus cedar tops the way amp builders talk about tube versus solid-state circuits — different material, different response to the same input. Back and sides matter too, but mainly for reflecting and coloring the sound the top has already generated, which is why rosewood's dense, reflective structure produces different overtones than maple's stiffer, more transparent one.
items: Spruce Top: Bright, clear tone with good projection
Cedar Top: Warm, woody tone with quick response
Mahogany Top: Focused midrange, vintage character
Rosewood Back/Sides: Rich overtones, powerful bass
Maple Back/Sides: Bright, punchy tone with clarity

cards.title: Pure Acoustic
cards.description: A pure acoustic has one job — resonate — so there's no preamp, battery, or under-saddle pickup to add weight, drain power, or eventually fail. That simplicity keeps the cost down and the tone entirely a function of the wood and construction, which is exactly what most players want for practicing at home or recording with a microphone rather than plugging in.

fields.label: Pros
fields.value: Lower cost, pure natural sound, no electronics to fail, lighter weight

fields.label: Best for
fields.value: Home playing, small venues, recording with mics

cards.title: Acoustic-Electric
cards.description: An acoustic-electric adds a pickup and preamp so the guitar's own resonance can be sent straight to a PA or interface, which matters the moment you need consistent volume on a stage where a microphone would also pick up monitor bleed and crowd noise. The onboard EQ is what makes that practical night to night, letting you compensate for a boomy room or thin-sounding venue without needing an outboard tone-shaping rig.

fields.label: Pros
fields.value: Can be amplified, great for live performance, built-in tuners often included, EQ controls

fields.label: Best for
fields.value: Live performance, recording direct, band settings

cards.title: Intermediate ($400-1200)
tableRows: Electronics, easy action, great for recording

cards.title: Daily Care
cards.description: Sweat and skin oil left on the strings after playing accelerates corrosion and dulls tone faster than the strings' own use would, so a quick wipe-down costs seconds but adds real string life. Humidity is the bigger long-term threat: solid wood tops expand and contract with moisture, and letting a guitar sit outside the 45-55% range for extended periods is how tops crack and bridges lift, not just how tone changes.
items: Wipe down strings after playing
Store in a case or on a stand
Keep away from extreme temperatures
Maintain 45-55% humidity
Loosen strings for long storage

cards.title: Periodic Maintenance
cards.description: Strings lose brightness gradually enough that most players don't notice the decline until they put on a fresh set and hear the difference, which is why changing them on a schedule rather than waiting for them to feel obviously dead keeps the guitar sounding its best. An annual setup catches the slower-moving problems — neck relief shifting with the seasons, intonation drifting — before they turn into buzzing or notes that won't stay in tune up the neck.
items: Change strings every 3-6 months
Professional setup annually
Check neck relief and intonation
Clean and condition fretboard
Polish body (avoid getting on strings)

cards.title: Fingerstyle Masters
cards.description: These players built entire careers on the idea that a single acoustic guitar, played with the fingers instead of a pick, can carry bass line, chords, and melody all at once — no band required.
items: Tommy Emmanuel
Chet Atkins
Andy McKee
Kaki King

cards.title: Singer-Songwriters
cards.description: For these artists the acoustic guitar is primarily a vehicle for the voice and the song, which is why their playing tends to prioritize steady, supportive rhythm over technical display.
items: Bob Dylan
Neil Young
Taylor Swift
Ed Sheeran

cards.title: Bluegrass/Country
cards.description: Bluegrass and country flatpickers use the acoustic guitar as a lead instrument, trading licks with fiddle and banjo, which demands the fast, precise picking and strong projection a good dreadnought is built to deliver.
items: Tony Rice
Norman Blake
Brad Paisley
Keith Whitley

cards.title: What to Look For
cards.description: A good acoustic should sound even across every string and up and down the neck — if one note dies faster than its neighbors or a certain fret buzzes only sometimes, that's usually a sign of an uneven fret job or a structural issue rather than something you can fix with technique. Playability matters just as much as tone, since a guitar that fights your fretting hand will quietly discourage practice no matter how good it sounds on its own.

fields.label: Sound Quality
fields.value: Clear, balanced tone across all strings; good sustain and projection; no buzzing or dead spots; harmonics ring clearly

fields.label: Playability
fields.value: Comfortable neck shape and width; appropriate string action height; easy fretting without excessive pressure; good intonation up the neck

cards.title: Red Flags to Avoid
cards.description: Some of these problems are cosmetic and some are structural, and telling them apart matters: a hairline finish crack is usually harmless, but a crack that runs across the grain of the top or back can mean the guitar was exposed to damaging humidity swings and may never sound quite right again. A neck that's visibly warped or twisted when you sight down it from the headstock is a repair job, not a quick setup fix, and is worth walking away from unless the price already reflects it.
items: High action that makes playing difficult
Visible cracks in the top or back
Buzzing that can't be fixed with setup
Warped or twisted neck
Loose or lifting bridge
Dead spots or notes that don't ring out
